subject: SignalPath reserved slab / SLO sizing — post-demo reconciliation
messages:
From: Camila Reyes <camila.reyes@redwood-inference.com>
To: Marta Lopéz <marta@signalpath.health>, eng@signalpath.health
Cc: ben.carter@redwood-inference.com
Date: Tue, 18 Jul 2028 15:02:00 -0700
Subject: SignalPath reserved slab / SLO sizing — post-demo reconciliation

Hi Marta / SignalPath eng team,

Great demo today — thanks for the time. I wanted to capture the items we agreed to and clarify a few workload specifics so our sizing proposal for a reserved capacity slab is accurate. Summary below (please correct anything I’ve mis-stated):

- Target production SLOs: 95th percentile tail latency <= 120ms for streaming user flows (token-at-a-time), and P50 <= 40ms for non-streaming bulk inference.
- Expected steady-state traffic: ~300 requests/sec peak, with 1.8 concurrency per user on average during bursts.
- Typical request length: median 80 tokens generated; worst-case up to 400 tokens for long-form clinical notes.
- KV cache warm rate: about 60% prefix reuse for common templates.
- Availability requirement: 99.9% monthly, with ability to burst 1.5x for up to 10 minutes during clinical shift changes.

Action items we promised to validate:
1) You to confirm average tokens-per-request and any heavy tail characteristics for long-form workflows (attached is the spreadsheet we’d like filled).
2) We’ll produce 3 slab options (reserved throughput per GPU configuration + fallback model variants) and an outline for a short validation run.
3) Decide whether streaming fidelity (per-token latency) or cost per token is the primary trade-off for early rollout.

I attached a lightweight SLO matrix to help collect missing numbers (signalpath-slo-matrix.xlsx). Once we have the workload numbers, Karthik will propose the hardware shortlist and a pilot plan.

Proposed timeline: you confirm numbers by EOD Thursday (20 Jul) — we’ll send slab options and a test plan by Monday (24 Jul).

Thanks,

Camila Reyes

Subject: Re: SignalPath reserved slab / SLO sizing — post-demo reconciliation

Camila,

Thanks — quick clarifications from our side:

- Peak req/s: 300 is correct over a sliding 5-minute window.
- Concurrency: typical concurrency per user is ~1.8, but simultaneous active sessions across the cluster can spike to ~650 concurrent active streams during shift overlap.
- Tokens: median outbound generated tokens is ~80; mean is ~120 due to some longer summaries. P99 requests hit ~380 tokens.
- Streaming: per-token latency is important for the triage UI — losing the felt snappiness at >180ms is a regression for our clinicians. So the 95th target of 120ms is what we need.
- Warm cache: about 55–65% reuse for standard templates; clinical templates are reused more heavily.

I’ve attached an exported slice of request metrics and a filled SLO worksheet. Please note we run a mix of high and low temperature models; the high-temperature paths (creative summarization) are the 10% heavy tail.

Best,
Marta

Marta Lopéz

From: Camila Reyes <camila.reyes@redwood-inference.com>
To: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood-inference.com>, ben.carter@redwood-inference.com
Cc: Marta Lopéz <marta@signalpath.health>, eng@signalpath.health
Date: Thu, 20 Jul 2028 08:34:00 -0700
Subject: SignalPath — slab options & validation asks (internal + external copy)

Karthik / Ben — looping you in with the filled numbers from SignalPath (attached). Key asks for sizing:

- Primary SLO: 95th streaming token latency <= 120ms at 300 req/s peak (with 650 concurrent active streams contingency).
- Workload mix: 90% standard templates (good prefix reuse), 10% long-form high-temperature summaries (heavy token count).

I sketched three candidate reserved-slab options to evaluate (high-level):

Option A — H100-80GB (single-model, higher single-request throughput):
- Reserved slab: 4 x H100-80GB
- Expected sustained throughput: ~1,200 req/s (assuming batching + streaming-friendly kernel), supports peak and buffer for bursts
- Pros: best single-thread latency, headroom for heavy-form requests
- Cons: higher cost, likely lower packing efficiency for tiny streaming requests without dynamic batching

Option B — A100-40GB (balanced):
- Reserved slab: 6 x A100-40GB
- Expected sustained throughput: ~1,000 req/s with better cost/per-token in mixed loads
- Pros: cost-effective for mixed workloads, good KV cache density
- Cons: slightly worse tail latency vs H100 under heavy concurrency

Option C — Quantized Ampere/T4 hybrid (cost-first):
- Reserved slab: 10 x T4 (or qA100 per SKU) with aggressive quantization + small-model fallback for heavy tails
- Expected sustained throughput: ~1,400 req/s in bulk (but potentially degraded streaming tail latency)
- Pros: lowest cost per token
- Cons: streaming per-token latency and fidelity risks for high-temp paths

Validation plan (short):
- 24–48 hour smoke pilot with synthetic traffic matching token distribution (include 10% heavy tail).
- Run per-GPU latency profiling for P50/P90/P95 streaming and non-streaming paths.
- Measure prefix cache hit effects by toggling template reuse fraction.
- Work with SignalPath eng to run a small A/B compare using real traffic in a throttled window (canary).

Please review the sizing math below and comment on assumptions I should alter. If you agree, I’ll propose a commercial slab (monthly reserved pricing) and the pilot dates to Marta.

Camila

Camila Reyes
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
camila.reyes@redwood-inference.com

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood-inference.com>
To: Camila Reyes <camila.reyes@redwood-inference.com>, Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood-inference.com>
Cc: Marta Lopéz <marta@signalpath.health>, eng@signalpath.health
Date: Mon, 22 Jul 2028 10:41:00 -0700
Subject: Re: SignalPath — slab options & validation asks (internal + external copy)

Camila / team / Marta,

Thanks for the clear workload numbers — I ran a quick sizing pass and recommend the H100-first slab with an A100 fallback as the most practical balance to hit the 95th streaming target of 120ms while giving predictable reserved throughput. Notes below:

Sizing/math (back of napkin):
- Streaming token latency target <= 120ms (95th). For our optimized streaming kernels, an H100-80GB can sustain ~300–350 concurrent lightweight streams with per-token median <= 35ms and P95 ~90–110ms (depends on sequence length and batch interleaving).
- Given 650 concurrent active streams worst-case, we estimate needing ~2.2 H100-equivalent capacity for headroom. Add 20% safety margin for KV cache cold-warm transitions and autoscaling buffer. => suggest 3 x H100-80GB as reserved baseline.
- For request-count / batching math: 300 req/s at median 80 tokens => ~24k tokens/sec. With streaming, batching is limited, so per-token kernel cost matters more than per-batch throughput. H100 gives better single-stream kernel latency.
- For heavy-tail (10% long-form) we recommend one of the H100s be provisioned with larger memory and higher burst threshold to avoid falling back to smaller quantized variants for these sessions.

Recommended reserved slab (final):
- Week 0 pilot: 1 x H100 + 2 x A100 (test hybrid headroom, validate P95 streaming across traffic mix)
- Production reserved slab: 3 x H100-80GB + 2 x A100-40GB as warm standby / cheaper non-stream fallback

Pilot test plan (concrete):
1) Synthetic replay run (24h): mirror token distribution and 10% heavy tail. Measure P50/P90/P95 per-token latency and throughput.
2) Prefix reuse test: toggle cache hit rate from 40% -> 70% during runs to quantify cost savings and tail improvements.
3) Canary: route 5% of real traffic during low-critical hours for 48h, monitor errors, latency, and user-perceived regressions.

Deliverables from our side: GPU latency matrix PDF, pilot run script, and a short runbook for canary rollback. I attached the latency matrix for the configurations above.

Next steps: Camila, if you can confirm SignalPath is OK with a short hybrid pilot (H100 + A100) we’ll prepare a price-backed reserved slab and schedule the pilot for the week of July 31.

Karthik Iyer
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
karthik.iyer@redwood-inference.com

Attachments: gpu-latency-matrix.pdf (pdf)
